gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured draw for a 5,000 BTU window AC. TechGearLab metered four 5,000 BTU units for one hour each on maximum settings and recorded 0.40–0.47 kWh, which is about 400–470 W. Set against named bench tests of the 3 kWh class (The Technology Man got 2,819 Wh from the BLUETTI Elite 300; Notebookcheck got about 2,650 Wh), that gives only 5.6–7.0 hours of flat-out cooling. Even the 3 kWh class needs the compressor to cycle to last 8 hours.
standout_why: I compared against the cited homepowerfacts.com and lightsonlab.com pages, plus testedwatts.com from the top results. homepowerfacts gets its 347 W draw by dividing by ENERGY STAR CEER, and its 'measured' usable-Wh column names no tester. It lists the Elite 200 V2 at 1,880, AC200L 1,680, AC180 950 and DELTA 2 Max 1,800, and does not list the Elite 300 or ALLPOWERS R4000. Lights On Lab labels its chart 'Calculated, not measured' and uses a 400–500 W range. Tested Watts uses retailer specs (LG LW5016 at 440 W) and says it has not tested. ChatGPT's second chat cited maker specs (GE 450 W, Danby 456 W). None of them has a metered AC draw, a named capacity test of the Elite 300, or the Elite 300's idle draw.
decides: This confirms the page's line that only the 3 kWh class can make it through a night, and it tightens the claim. With a conventional 5,000 BTU unit at TechGearLab's measured 400–470 W, the best-measured 3 kWh unit (Elite 300) delivers 2,650–2,819 Wh, about 5.6–7.0 hours of continuous cooling. It gets through 8 hours only if the compressor cycles, at roughly 75–85 % run time or less, or with an inverter AC. Every 2 kWh unit with a named measurement (DELTA 2 Max 1,800 Wh, Elite 200 V2 1,910 Wh) gives about 4–4.8 hours at 400 W. The AC180 (950–1,030 Wh) gives about 2.4–2.6 hours. So the picks stay Elite 300 and R4000, and the 2 kWh rows should be labelled 'half a night'. Leaving the AC outlet on also costs about 19 W of idle draw (The Technology Man), roughly 150 Wh over 8 hours.
